mainTopic: Who may take on private fasts, practical fasting rules, and advice for travelers drawn from the story of יוסף and his brothers.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא: individuals do not fast on the festive days listed in מגילת תענית. A ברייתא then teaches that every תלמיד חכם counts as a יחיד for private fasts, and defines a יחיד and a תלמיד. Two more ברייתות record a מחלוקת about whether an ordinary person may take on these practices. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל concludes that one may not take on things that bring honor, but may take on things that bring hardship. Next come practical fasting rules: finish a fast even if its reason has passed, a traveler fasts if either town is fasting, and one who ate by mistake should not show it in public. Lessons from the story of יוסף and his brothers follow. רבי אלעזר warns against deep הלכה study on the road, and the גמרא reconciles this with the teaching that travelers must talk Torah: reviewing is fine, deep analysis is not. A ברייתא adds advice against long strides and for traveling only in daylight. The amud ends with רבי חייא's rule that a traveler should eat lightly, two reasons for it, and the start of the difference between them, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: No individual fasts on the holidays of מגילת תענית
steps.stepSummary: The last item in an ongoing list: individuals may not fast on the festive days recorded in מגילת תענית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And on the festive days that are written in מגילת תענית.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes a ברייתא that began on the previous amud, listing days when individuals may not decree fasts. The last item is the festive days listed in מגילת תענית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though יחידים are allowed to take on fasts, some days are off-limits. מגילת תענית lists days on which the חכמים forbade fasting because good things happened to the Jewish people on them.

keyTerms.meaning: An ancient list of dates on which fasting was forbidden because of joyous historical events

phrases.english: And on festive days
that are written in Megillat Taanit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ברייתא begun earlier about days when individual fasts are not held.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Individuals do not fast on the festive days recorded in מגילת תענית.

steps.title: Every Torah scholar counts as an individual for fasting
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a person should not hold back from fasting as a יחיד by claiming he is only a תלמיד. All תלמידי חכמים are יחידים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A person should not say, 'I am only a student, so I am not fit to be a יחיד.' Rather, all Torah scholars are יחידים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about who should take part in the special fasts of the יחידים mentioned in the משנה. It tells a modest scholar not to excuse himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think the title יחיד is only for great sages, so a humble learner should stay out. The ברייתא rejects this. Any תלמיד חכם is included in the group of יחידים who fast.

keyTerms.meaning: An individual of special standing who takes on extra fasts

steps.confusionAlert: Here יחיד does not mean just 'one person.' It is a title for a person of spiritual standing who fasts on behalf of the community.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A person should not say: I am a student,
I am not worthy to be an individual,
rather: all Torah scholars are individuals.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אַל יֹאמַר אָדָם תַּלְמִיד אֲנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion about who counts as a יחיד for fasting.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every תלמיד חכם is considered a יחיד for the purpose of fasting.

steps.title: What is the difference between an individual and a student?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks for definitions of the two terms it just used.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who is a יחיד, and who is a תלמיד?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא pauses to ask what exactly a יחיד is and what a תלמיד is. This sets up the definitions in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous line mentioned both levels without explaining them. Before going further, we need to know where the line between the two is drawn.

phrases.english: Who is an individual and who is a student?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for definitions of the terms used in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The definitions of יחיד and תלמיד.

steps.title: Defining the individual and the student
steps.stepSummary: A יחיד is someone fit to be appointed a communal leader. A תלמיד is someone who can answer a halachic question on what he has learned, even if only in the tractate studied during the כלה month.
steps.simpleTranslation: A יחיד is anyone fit to be appointed a leader over the community. A תלמיד is anyone who, when asked a halachic question in what he has learned, can answer it, even if only in the tractate of the כלה gathering.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question with two definitions. A יחיד is the higher level and a תלמיד is the lower level.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A יחיד must be learned enough to be a פרנס, a leader and teacher of the community. A תלמיד only needs to answer correctly within his own learning, even if that is just the one tractate everyone studied at the יַרְחֵי כַלָּה gathering. So the bar for תלמיד is quite low.

keyTerms.meaning: A leader appointed over the community
The tractate studied publicly during the כלה months

phrases.english: An individual: anyone who is worthy
to be appointed leader over the community;
a student: anyone whom they ask
a matter of law in his learning and he answers,
and even in the tractate of the kallah gathering.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָחִיד — כֹּל שֶׁרָאוּי לְמַנּוֹתוֹ פַּרְנָס עַל הַצִּבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A יחיד is someone fit to lead the community. A תלמיד is someone who can answer halachic questions in his own learning, even if only in the כלה tractate.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two levels. A יחיד is fit to lead the community. A תלמיד can answer questions in what he learned. Both count for the fasts of יחידים.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: not everyone may take on these practices
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר holds that not every person who wants to act as a יחיד or a תלמיד may do so.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Not everyone who wants to make himself a יחיד may do so, and the same goes for a תלמיד. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא asks whether an ordinary person may adopt the practices of a יחיד or a תלמיד on his own initiative. רבי מאיר says no.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern is that someone who is not truly qualified would be taking on a status he does not deserve. To רבי מאיר, that looks like showing off.
steps.confusionAlert: The words 'תלמיד — עושה' literally say 'a student does.' One reading, which this breakdown follows, carries the negative over: just as not everyone may act as a יחיד, not everyone may act as a תלמיד. Another possible reading takes the words at face value: an ordinary person may not make himself a יחיד, but a תלמיד may.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא כׇּל הָרוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת עַצְמוֹ יָחִיד עוֹשֶׂה,
phrases.english: Not everyone who wishes to make himself an individual may do so,
[nor everyone who wishes to act as] a student may do so,
phrases.notes: The negative 'not everyone' carries over to this clause

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא כׇּל הָרוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת עַצְמוֹ יָחִיד עוֹשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the levels are defined, asks whether one may adopt them on his own.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Per רבי מאיר, an unqualified person may not adopt the practices of a יחיד or a תלמיד.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: one may, and is praised for it
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי disagrees: a person may take on these practices and is remembered for good, because they bring him hardship, not honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: He may do so, and he is remembered for good, because it is not praise for him but pain for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי argues with רבי מאיר and allows an ordinary person to act like a יחיד or a תלמיד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר's worry was showing off. רבי יוסי answers that taking on extra fasts is a hardship (צער), not a source of honor. So there is no arrogance here, only extra devotion, and it is praiseworthy.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
he may do so, and he is remembered for good,
because it is not praise for him,
but rather it is pain for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: עוֹשֶׂה, וְזָכוּר לַטּוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes רבי מאיר's ruling in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Per רבי יוסי, one may adopt these practices and is praised, since they are hardship, not honor.

steps.title: Another ברייתא: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר takes the strict view
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא gives the same strict ruling in the name of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: Not everyone who wants to make himself a יחיד may do so, and the same goes for a תלמיד. These are the words of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a parallel ברייתא with the same strict opinion, here said by רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. This sets up a different response in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording is the same as רבי מאיר's. What is new is the speaker and the different kind of disagreement that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: It is taught in another ברייתא
A תנא, student of רבי מאיר

phrases.english: It is taught in another baraita:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא כׇּל הָרוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת עַצְמוֹ יָחִיד עוֹשֶׂה,
phrases.english: Not everyone who wishes to make himself an individual may do so,
[nor everyone who wishes to act as] a student may do so,
these are the words of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: לֹא כׇּל הָרוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת עַצְמוֹ יָחִיד עוֹשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel version of the ברייתא from step 5, with a different speaker.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Per רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, not everyone may adopt the status of a יחיד or a תלמיד.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: honor is restricted, hardship is allowed
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל limits the restriction to practices that bring honor. Practices that bring hardship, like fasting, anyone may take on, and he is remembered for good.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: When was this said? For something that brings honor. But for something that brings hardship, he may do it and is remembered for good, because it is not praise for him but pain for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל does not reject the strict ruling outright. He limits it: the ban applies only to honorable practices, while practices of hardship are open to all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses בַּמֶּה דְּבָרִים אֲמוּרִים to narrow the earlier ruling. Wearing a scholar's distinguished clothing is forbidden for an ordinary person, because it brings honor. Taking on extra fasts is allowed and praiseworthy, because it brings hardship. This brings out the reasoning behind רבי יוסי's view as well.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case were these words said? (a formula for limiting a ruling)

steps.whatToRemember: The key test is honor versus hardship. A person may not claim the honors of a יחיד or a תלמיד, but he may take on their hardships, like extra fasting, and is praised for it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a general principle for taking on extra strictness: it is proper when it brings self-sacrifice, but not when it brings status.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
In what case were these words said?
In a matter of praise,
but in a matter of pain, he may do so,
and he is remembered for good,
for it is not praise for him,
but rather it is pain for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: בַּמֶּה דְּבָרִים אֲמוּרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's ruling to matters of honor only.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The restriction applies only to honorable practices. Anyone may take on practices of hardship and is remembered for good.

steps.title: The reason for the fast went away, but he still finishes
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if someone fasted over a trouble that passed, or over a sick person who got better, he still completes his fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: if someone was fasting over a trouble and the trouble passed, or over a sick person and the person got better, he keeps fasting and completes the fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that opens a new set of practical fasting rules. The first rule covers a fast whose reason disappears partway through the day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think the fast stops once its reason is gone. The ברייתא says no: once a person has started a fast, he finishes it. The good news does not cancel the fast he already took on.

keyTerms.meaning: He fasts and completes the fast

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁהָיָה מִתְעַנֶּה עַל הַצָּרָה וְעָבְרָה,
phrases.english: One who was fasting over a trouble, and it passed,
or over a sick person, and he was healed —
he fasts and completes the fast.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from who may take on private fasts to practical rules for keeping a fast.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fast that was started is completed even if its reason went away.

steps.title: Traveling between a fasting town and a non-fasting town
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that a traveler follows the stricter practice. He fasts if either his old town or his new town is fasting.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone goes from a place that is not fasting to a place that is fasting, he fasts with them. If he goes from a place that is fasting to a place that is not fasting, he completes his fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with two travel cases. In both, the traveler ends up fasting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a fasting town, he joins the local people so he does not stand apart from them. If he left a fasting town, he still keeps the fast he was obligated in back home. So whichever town is fasting makes him fast.

keyTerms.meaning: A place where they are fasting

phrases.english: One who goes from a place where they are not fasting
to a place where they are fasting —
he fasts with them.
From a place where they are fasting to a place where they are not fasting —
he fasts and completes the fast.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a new case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A traveler fasts if either his old town or his new town is fasting.

steps.title: He forgot and ate on the fast day
steps.stepSummary: Someone who forgot and ate on a fast day must not show himself full in public or treat himself to luxuries. This is learned from יעקב's warning to his sons.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he forgot and ate and drank, he should not show himself in front of the community, and he should not treat himself to luxuries. The verse says: 'And יעקב said to his sons: why should you show yourselves?' יעקב told his sons: do not show yourselves full in front of עשו or ישמעאל, so that they do not become jealous of you.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives one more rule, for someone who ate by mistake on a fast day. It brings a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating by mistake does not turn the day into a regular day. He should still hold back and not act full in front of people who are fasting. During the famine, יעקב warned his sons not to look well-fed in front of hungry neighbors. The same idea applies here: don't flaunt being full in front of people who are going without.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does not say his fast is over and he can now eat freely. He still behaves like someone fasting, at least in front of other people.

phrases.english: If he forgot and ate and drank —
he should not show himself before the community,
and he should not indulge himself in luxuries,
as it says: "And Jacob said to his sons: Why do you show yourselves?"
Jacob said to his sons:
Do not show yourselves when you are full,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא בִּפְנֵי עֵשָׂו וְלֹא בִּפְנֵי יִשְׁמָעֵאל,
phrases.english: not before Esau and not before Ishmael,
so that they will not be jealous of you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final rule of the same ברייתא, with a פסוק as its source.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who ate by mistake on a fast day should not appear full in public or treat himself to luxuries.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's rules: finish a fast even if its reason passed; a traveler fasts if either town is fasting; if you ate by mistake, don't show it off.

steps.title: יוסף tells his brothers not to learn הלכה on the road
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains the פסוק 'אל תרגזו בדרך': יוסף told his brothers not to get involved in הלכה while traveling.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Do not be troubled on the way.' רבי אלעזר said: יוסף told his brothers, do not get busy with a matter of הלכה, or the road may become troublesome for you.
steps.whatsHappening: Having quoted one lesson from the story of יוסף and his brothers, the גמרא brings another. רבי אלעזר explains what יוסף meant when he sent them home.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר reads 'אל תרגזו' as a warning about Torah discussion on a journey. Deep focus on a הלכה can distract a traveler, so he loses his way or gets into trouble on the road. Sefaria understands it as getting into an argument instead.

phrases.english: "Do not be troubled on the way"
Rabbi Elazar said,
Joseph said to his brothers:
Do not occupy yourselves with a matter of halakha,
lest the road become troublesome for you.
phrases.notes: Either you get distracted and lose your way, or you fall into an argument (Sefaria).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connected by theme: another lesson from the story of יוסף and his brothers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Travelers should not get involved in הלכה discussion on the road.

steps.title: Challenge: Torah talk on the road protects you
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אלעזר using רבי אלעאי בר ברכיה. He says two תלמידי חכמים walking without Torah talk deserve to be burned, learned from אליהו and אלישע.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבי אלעאי בר ברכיה said: two תלמידי חכמים who walk on the road with no Torah talk between them deserve to be burned. The verse says: 'They were walking and talking, and a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them.' The reason they were safe is that they were talking. If there had been no talking, they would have deserved to be burned!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי אלעזר's reading from step 12. Another אמורא teaches the very opposite: Torah talk on the road is required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אליהו and אלישע were walking and 'talking', which means Torah talk. Because of that, the fiery chariot only separated them and did not burn them. So Torah talk while traveling protects you. That clashes with the idea that you should avoid הלכה on the road. The answer comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason is because there is (sets up an inference)

phrases.english: Is that so?
But didn't Rabbi Elai bar Berekhya say:
Two Torah scholars who are walking on the road
and there are no words of Torah between them —
they deserve to be burned,
as it says: "And it was, as they went on walking and talking,
phrases.notes: מלכים ב ב:יא, about אליהו and אלישע

phrases.english: and behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire
and they separated the two of them".
The reason is that there was talk,
but if there was no talk —
they would deserve to be burned!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אִלְעַאי בַּר בֶּרֶכְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly challenges רבי אלעזר's statement in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's teaching that one should not get involved in הלכה while traveling.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעאי בר ברכיה reads the פסוק about אליהו and אלישע to show that Torah talk on the road is required and protects you. Skipping it makes one deserve burning, which contradicts the advice to avoid הלכה on the road.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the next passage, where the גמרא will separate two kinds of Torah learning to resolve the contradiction.

steps.title: Reviewing is fine on the road; deep analysis is not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. רבי אלעאי בר ברכיה means reviewing learning you already know. רבי אלעזר means analyzing הלכה in depth.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is about reviewing by heart. That one is about analyzing in depth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 13 by showing that the two statements are talking about two different kinds of learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעאי בר ברכיה wants travelers to talk Torah. That means reviewing (גירסא), which is safe while walking. רבי אלעזר warned against getting involved in הלכה on the road. That means deep analysis (עיון), which can cause arguments or make you lose your way. Both rules stand, each in its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the contradiction can be resolved
To review by rote, going over what you already learned

steps.whatToRemember: While traveling, review Torah (גירסא), but avoid deep analysis (עיון).

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one is about reviewing,
phrases.notes: Refers to רבי אלעאי בר ברכיה

phrases.english: that one is about analyzing in depth.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא — לְמִיגְרַס, הָא — לְעַיּוֹנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (two kinds of learning)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It looked as if רבי אלעזר forbids all Torah talk on the road.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only deep analysis is discouraged. Reviewing is encouraged.

steps.title: A ברייתא: no long strides, and arrive before sunset
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא adds two more pieces of advice that יוסף gave his brothers for their journey.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: Do not take long strides, and bring the sun into the city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives a different reading of יוסף's words 'אל תרגזו בדרך'. It lists two travel tips, and the next steps explain each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a second reading of the same פסוק. Instead of being about Torah study, it is about practical safety on the road. 'Bring the sun into the city' means: get to the city while the sun is still up.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
Bring the sun into the city, meaning arrive before sunset

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita:
Do not take long strides,
and bring the sun into the city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another reading of the פסוק that רבי אלעזר explained
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A traveler should not take long strides and should reach the city before sunset.

steps.title: Why long strides are harmful
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that a long stride takes away 1/500 of a person's eyesight.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Do not take long strides': as the Master said, a long stride takes away one five-hundredth of a person's eyesight.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first half of the ברייתא by giving the reason behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rushing on the road with big strides seems to save time. But the גמרא says it physically harms you by weakening your eyesight. So hurrying is not worth it.

keyTerms.meaning: As the Master said; quoting a known teaching

phrases.english: Do not take long strides:
as the Master said:
a long stride takes away
one five-hundredth
of a person's eyesight.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first clause of the ברייתא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Long strides harm the eyesight, so a traveler should avoid them.

steps.title: Leave and arrive in daylight
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב teaches that a person should leave and enter a place only while it is light ('כי טוב'). The proof is the פסוק about יוסף's brothers leaving in the morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And bring the sun into the city': this follows רב יהודה in the name of רב, who said: A person should always leave with 'it is good' and enter with 'it is good,' as it says: 'The morning was light, and the men were sent away.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second half of the ברייתא by connecting it to a general rule of רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'כי טוב' is the phrase the Torah uses about light at creation, so here it means daylight. Traveling in the dark is dangerous. יוסף's brothers were sent off only once morning came, and this shows that we leave in daylight. The same goes for entering a city.

keyTerms.meaning: In line with the teaching of רב יהודה
Always; a general rule of conduct
'That it is good', a code word for daylight (from בראשית 1:4)
As it says; introduces a פסוק as proof

steps.confusionAlert: 'כי טוב' here is not about something being 'good' in general. It is a way of saying 'when it is light.'

phrases.english: And bring the sun into the city:
this is like what Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav.
For Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
A person should always leave with 'it is good' (daylight)
and enter with 'it is good' (daylight),
as it is said:
'The morning was light,
and the men were sent away.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second clause of the ברייתא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Travel only in daylight, both when leaving and when entering a place.
steps.whatToRemember: יוסף's travel advice: don't rush with long strides, and travel only by daylight.

steps.title: A traveler should eat lightly
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רבי חייא: someone on the road should not eat more than he would in years of famine.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רבי חייא: One who travels on the road should not eat more than in years of famine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another piece of travel advice, this time about eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is to eat small, famine-sized portions while traveling. The reason is not given yet. The גמרא will ask for it next.

keyTerms.meaning: One who travels on the road

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Chiya:
One who walks on the road
should not eat more
than in years of famine.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new travel guideline, following the earlier travel advice
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A traveler eats only famine-sized portions.

steps.title: Why eat less on the road?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבי חייא's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a traveler should eat less. This sets up the two answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a real question, not an attack. The גמרא wants to understand what the rule is based on.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind Step 18
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for eating little while traveling

steps.title: Two reasons: health or saving food
steps.stepSummary: In בבל they explained it is for the digestion. In ארץ ישראל they said it is so the food supply lasts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here they explained: because of the bowels. In the West they say: because of the food supply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two different explanations for the rule, one from בבל and one from ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason is about health: walking hard on a full stomach can harm the digestion. The second reason is practical: if you eat a lot, your food may run out before the trip ends. Both reasons give the same rule, but they come from different concerns.

keyTerms.meaning: In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Here (in Babylonia) they explained:
because of the bowels.
phrases.notes: A full stomach can be harmed by the strain of travel

phrases.english: In the West (Eretz Yisrael) they say:
because of the food supply.
phrases.notes: So the provisions last the whole trip

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 19
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: בבל: for health of the digestion. ארץ ישראל: to save food.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two reasons?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the two reasons, and begins its answer: 'there is a difference between them.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them? There is a difference between them:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It asks in what case the two reasons would lead to different results, and it starts to answer. The answer continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When two reasons are given for the same rule, the גמרא often looks for a case where only one of them applies. The words 'איכא בינייהו' open the answer, which comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the practical difference between them?
There is a difference between them; opens the answer

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?
There is a difference between them:
phrases.notes: The answer continues on the next amud

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two reasons given in Step 20
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where the two reasons lead to different results
